title: Mount Rainier Lahars- Hazards for the Puyallup and Nisqually River Drainages
description:
Large lahars (volcanic mudflows) pose substantial threats to people and property downstream from Mount Rainier, Washington. Lahars can occur during an eruption, as happened at Mount St. Helens on May 18, 1980. Lahars can also begin as large landslides that occur without warning, traveling down river channels to densely populated areas downstream.
To inform potentially affected communities, assist school districts with implementing state mandatory lahar drills, and help emergency management officials prepare for the possibility of a large lahar, the USGS prepared state-of-the-art numerical simulations (D-Claw) of hypothetical lahars that originate as landslides high on Mount Rainier’s western flank and descend the Puyallup and Nisqually River valleys.
The simulations focused on the Sunset Amphitheater and Tahoma Glacier Headwall, areas identified as the most landslide-prone part of the volcano. Two different volumes were modeled: 260 million cubic meters, the approximate volume of the Electron Mudflow that occurred at Mount Rainier about 500 years ago, and 52 million cubic meters, the volume of a large landslide that occurred at Mount Meager volcano, British Columbia, in 2010. The computer model predicted how flow would move across the terrain if it consisted of a fairly dense (hard) rock mass (the low mobility scenario) and how the flow would behave if it consisted of weakened, clay-rich rock (the high mobility scenario). The simulations predict inundation patterns, depths, and speeds of lahars for landslides of different volumes and mobilities, information not available in a prior hazards assessment report.
The report confirms our general understanding of lahar threats and analyses of lahar velocity, depths, and areas of inundation in the present USGS hazard assessment and related hazard documents. The results provide needed information for the continued development of evacuation routes, and general emergency response plans.
The report does not predict when the next large lahar will occur. It provides examples of how lahars of differing sizes and mobilities could behave. The simulations rely on decades of research on the geology of Mount Rainier, the physics of landslide initiation and lahar dynamics, and computational methods for computer simulations.
Open-file Report 2021-1118, "Modeling the Dynamics of Lahars that Originate as Landslides on the West Side of Mount Rainier, Washington", is authored by USGS scientists David George, Richard Iverson, and Charles Cannon of the USGS Cascades Volcano Observatory and USGS Oregon Water Science Center.

transcript.text: USGS scientists studying Mount Rainier have long recognized that the greatest hazard posed
by the volcano is from landslides that begin high on its slopes and transform into mud flows
or lahars that travel great distances down river valleys.
Lahars are rapidly moving flows of water, mud and rock.
They can move almost as fluidly as water, yet be as dense as wet concrete.
Lahars can vary or carry away nearly everything in their paths and leave behind a layer of hard
rocky sediment.
Large lahars commonly accompany volcanic eruptions, but they can also develop from landslides that
occur without eruptive activity or any warning, making it very important that people understand
lahar behavior and hazards.
USGS scientists and mathematicians teamed up to develop state-of-the-art computer simulations
that show what happens when large landslides on Mount Rainier's western flank transform into
lahars and descend into the Puyallup and Nisquale River valleys.
The simulations show where and how far the lahars can go, when they arrive, and how deep
the lahar would be.
This simulation starts with a landslide in the Sunset Amphitheater area.
The timer shows a lapse time after the landslide begins.
The colors represent depths.
White yellow is less than 3 feet.
Dark red is more than 150 feet.
In this scenario, 260 million cubic meters of rock and ice, a volume similar in size to
the electron mudflow that occurred at Mount Rainier about 500 years ago, slides off the
volcano.
If the material is dense hard rock, the landslide stabilizes before flowing very far.
This is the low mobility scenario and it never reaches communities downstream.
But if the rock is weak and has a lot of clay, the landslide will transform into a highly
mobile, swift-moving lahar.
Part of the lahar flows south and enters the Nisquale River valley, but most of it moves
into the Puyallup River drainage.
The lahar reaches the town of Ording in about 50 minutes.
The lahar slows and spreads across the wide valley between the Puyallup and Carbon Rivers.
The shades of orange represent depths of 6 to 16 feet.
Along the river corridors, it is much deeper.
After passing through Ording, the lahar continues to the Sumner and Puyallup lowlands, arriving
in 3 to 4 hours after the landslide begins.
The lahar was slow and come to rest in 4 to 5 hours, but the deposit may remain liquefied
for many more hours and flooding may occur downstream.
This next simulation starts with the collapse of the steep cliffs of the De Homa Glacier
head wall.
The timer shows a lapse time after the landslide begins.
The colors represent depths.
Light yellow is less than 3 feet.
Dark red is more than 150 feet.
In this scenario, 260 million cubic meters of rock and ice slides off the volcano.
If it is mainly dense, hard rock.
The landslide stabilizes before flowing very far.
This is the low mobility scenario that never reaches communities downstream.
But if the rock is rich in clay, the landslide will transform into a highly mobile, swift-moving
lahar.
The lahar that travels down the Puyallup River drainage will arrive in Ording in a little
over 60 minutes.
There, it slows and spreads out across the wide valley.
After passing through Ording, the lahar continues to the Sumner and Puyallup lowlands.
The lahar that travels down the Nisqually River drainage will arrive at the National Park boundary
in about 5 minutes and the community of Ashford in about 15 minutes.
The lahar reaches the Alder Lake Reservoir in about 50 minutes.
The lahar begins filling the upper end of Alder Lake.
The sediment-rich lahar, which is the brown color, mixes with lake water, which is blue.
The lahar doesn't generate a substantial wave.
Instead, over the next 50 minutes, the lake level slowly rises.
About an hour and a half after the landslide begins, water starts overtopping the Alder
Lake dam.
The computer simulation ends two hours after the landslide begins and does not address what
happens to the dam when water begins flowing over it or what might occur downstream of the
dam.
We do not know when the next large lahar at Mount Rainier will occur or how big it will
be.
These computer simulations provide estimated lahar travel times and depths, so emergency
officials and communities in lahar-hazard zones can continue to take the steps necessary
to prepare for a future lahar by developing alert systems and evacuation routes that lead
away from valley floors.
You can do more by following three steps.
Learn, inquire, plan.
First, learn about the volcanoes and hazards that could affect you.
Second, talk to local officials about their plans to handle a volcano emergency.
Third, develop a family preparedness and communications plan and a kit with emergency provisions.
Know how to access information during an emergency and be ready to act.
If you are at risk from lahar's and are aware that one is in progress, move rapidly
off the valley floor.
